name: cat
summary: Print whole files to the terminal, or join several files together.
compat: -n works in BusyBox. -A is GNU; BusyBox offers -v -e -t for similar output.

examples.title: Print a short file
examples.explain: Best for short files. For long files use less, head or tail so the start does not scroll away.

examples.title: Number the lines
examples.explain: Useful when a compiler error mentions a line number.

examples.title: Reveal tabs and Windows line endings
examples.explain: Tabs show as ^I, line ends as $ and Windows carriage returns as ^M. Explains 'missing separator' Makefile errors (spaces instead of a tab) and '/bin/bash^M: bad interpreter'.

examples.title: Join two files into a new file
examples.explain: Prints file1 then file2 and redirects the result into a new file.
examples.warning: > empties <combined-file> first if it already exists. Never use one of the input files as the output: it gets truncated before it is read.
options: Write output to a file, replacing its contents

name: less
summary: Scroll and search through long files or command output, one screen at a time.

install.note: BusyBox provides a basic less; very small systems may only have more.

compat: Keys: Space/PageDown next page, b back, /text search forward, n next match, G end, g start, q quit.

examples.title: Open a file for reading
examples.explain: less never modifies the file. Press h inside less for the full list of keys.

examples.title: Page through command output
examples.explain: The pipe sends the output of the first command into less. Add 2>&1 before the pipe to include error messages too, e.g. make 2>&1 | less.
options: Pipe: connect standard output of the left command to the input of the right one

examples.title: Show line numbers
examples.explain: Prefixes every line with its number.

examples.title: Follow a growing log file
examples.explain: Like tail -f, but press Ctrl+C to stop following and scroll or search, then F to resume following.

name: head
summary: Print the first lines (or bytes) of a file or of command output.
compat: -n and -c are POSIX/BusyBox compatible. The old form head -20 still works in most implementations but -n 20 is clearer.

examples.title: Limit long command output
examples.explain: Shows only the first lines of output; common after sort to get a 'top 5'.

name: tail
summary: Print the last lines of a file, or follow a log file as new lines are written.
compat: -f works in BusyBox; -F (follow by name, survive log rotation) is GNU and newer BusyBox.

examples.title: Last 50 lines of a log
examples.explain: The most recent entries in a log file are at the end.
options: Number of lines from the end

examples.title: Watch a log live
examples.explain: Keeps printing new lines as they are appended. Press Ctrl+C to stop; that only stops tail, not the program writing the log.
options: Follow: keep reading as the file grows

examples.title: Follow a log that gets rotated
examples.explain: Like -f but reopens the file if it is replaced by log rotation.
options: Follow by name and retry if the file disappears

examples.title: Count lines in a file
examples.explain: Using < (input redirection) prints just the number; wc -l notes.txt prints the number followed by the file name.
options: Feed the file to the command's standard input

examples.title: Count results of another command
examples.explain: Counts how many lines the first command printed, here the number of .c files below the current directory.

name: diff
summary: Show the differences between two files or two directories.
compat: Exit status: 0 = identical, 1 = different, 2 = trouble (e.g. file missing). Scripts can test it with if diff -q a b >/dev/null; then ...

examples.title: Unified diff of two files
examples.explain: Lines starting with - exist only in the old file, + only in the new file; @@ lines show the line ranges. This is the same format git diff and patch use.
options: Unified format with 3 lines of context

test.before: cp notes.txt notes2.txt && echo 'extra line' >> notes2.txt

examples.title: Only say whether files differ
examples.explain: Prints nothing if identical. Use -r with two directories to compare whole trees.

name: od
summary: Dump a file as hexadecimal bytes, to see binary data or hidden characters.
compat: od is in coreutils and BusyBox everywhere. Alternatives: hexdump -C (util-linux or BusyBox) and xxd (ships with vim). The z suffix in -t x1z is a GNU extension.

examples.title: Hex and ASCII side by side
examples.explain: Left column is the offset in hex, then each byte in hex, then printable characters between > <. head keeps a large binary from flooding the terminal.
options: Show 1-byte hex values plus printable characters (GNU)
Do not collapse repeated lines into *

examples.title: Show the first 16 bytes of a binary
examples.explain: An ELF file starts with 7f 45 4c 46 (\x7f then 'ELF'). Checking the first bytes is a quick way to identify file formats and image headers.
